strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in robust visual recognition: improving minority-group performance while controlling sensitivity to parameter perturbations. The proposed combination of SAM perturbations and Group DRO weighting is simple and potentially useful when group annotations are available.

Waterbirds provides a controlled improvement over GDRO with the same regularization strength: worst-group accuracy increases from 86.5% to 87.2%, and group-average accuracy increases from 90.4% to 90.6%. Both minority groups improve, and experiments use five random seeds.

Table 2 provides supporting evidence for reduced local curvature relative to GDRO: SGDRO lowers both reported Hessian eigenvalues across every group, with the overall largest eigenvalue decreasing from 356.6 to 268.7.

Evaluation extends beyond Waterbirds to six DomainBed datasets. The reported average accuracy is 71.4%, versus 70.1% for GDRO and 70.9% for ERM. Reporting three seeds and using training-domain validation for model selection are positive experimental practices.
weaknesses: The claimed guarantees of common flat minima and worst-group generalization are not established. Section 3.1 provides only a local Taylor argument. For a fixed worst group, the implemented direction expands as ∇L_g + ρH_g∇L_S/||∇L_S||, whereas the manuscript writes the overall-loss gradient and Hessian while describing them as group-specific. Missing group indices may be repairable notation, but the corrected expansion still provides no guarantee of flatness or generalization under distribution shift. The test-loss Hessian measurements establish a curvature observation, not these guarantees.

The relationship between Equation 4 and Algorithm 1 is mathematically incomplete. The perturbation ε*(θ) depends on θ, but the algorithm omits its derivative when updating parameters. Because the perturbation is selected using overall loss while the outer objective uses group losses, it does not solve the corresponding inner maximization, and an envelope-theorem justification does not directly apply. The manuscript needs to identify and justify this approximation before treating the update as optimization of the stated objective.

The distinguishing design choice is insufficiently validated. There is no comparison between perturbations computed from overall loss, worst-group loss, and the adversarially weighted group loss, nor an ablation of updating group weights at clean versus perturbed parameters. SAM is also absent from the DomainBed comparison. Consequently, the results do not establish the value of this particular coupling beyond combining two existing methods. Together with the unsupported theoretical claims, this is the main reason the balance favors weak rejection despite the useful empirical gains.

The performance interpretation overstates the evidence. In Table 1, weighted average accuracy decreases from 93.8% to 93.1%, and both majority groups worsen relative to GDRO; this does not demonstrate the claimed alleviation of majority-group degradation. The 0.7-point worst-group gain is modest, and the meaning of the Waterbirds error bars is unspecified. Table 3 reports average domain-generalization accuracy rather than worst-domain performance, so it does not directly substantiate broader worst-case claims.

Experimental attribution and reproducibility remain incomplete. Waterbirds uses an L2 penalty of 1.0 for GDRO/SGDRO but 0.0001 for ERM/SAM, so explanations of ordinary SAM's minority-group sharpness are confounded by regularization, although the GDRO–SGDRO comparison is controlled. Important implementation details are largely delegated to prior work: the backbone and pretraining configuration, minibatch group sampling, handling of absent groups, and DomainBed perturbation-radius search space are not explicitly specified. No implementation link or complete configuration is supplied.
